passages.happening:
When it is decided that ‘we’ will sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners are handed over to a centurion named Julius, of the Imperial Regiment (verse 1). They board a ship from Adramyttium, bound for ports along the coast of Asia. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, is with them (verse 2). At Sidon, Julius kindly lets Paul visit his friends and be cared for (verse 3).

The winds are against them, so they sail on the sheltered side of Cyprus (verse 4), across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, to Myra in Lycia (verse 5). There the centurion finds an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and puts them on board (verse 6). They sail slowly for many days and with difficulty reach Cnidus. The wind holds them back, so they sail in the shelter of Crete, past Salmone (verse 7), and with difficulty reach a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The ‘we’ has come back. The writer is on the ship again, as in the earlier ‘we’ passages, and many think it is Luke himself. This chapter is told by someone who was there.

Paul is a prisoner, but not alone. Aristarchus, from Thessalonica, sails with him. Paul later calls him ‘my fellow prisoner’ (Colossians 4:10). And the centurion, Julius, treats Paul well from the start, letting him go ashore at Sidon to see friends who could give him what he needed for a long voyage.

The route shows how ships worked in that world. The first ship was a coasting vessel from Adramyttium, a port in the north-west of the province of Asia, working its way from harbour to harbour. At Myra, on the south coast of what is now Turkey, Julius moved his prisoners to a ship from Alexandria in Egypt bound for Italy. Rome lived on grain shipped from Egypt and North Africa, and this was probably one of the grain ships that fed the city; verse 38 says it carried grain.

The winds were against them all the way. Ships of that time could not sail well into the wind. Cnidus lay at the south-west tip of what is now Turkey. From there, instead of crossing straight to the west, they had to run south and creep along the sheltered southern coast of Crete. Fair Havens was a small bay on that coast. Every stage took longer than it should, and time was running out.
passages.ot:
The sea in the Old Testament is a place of danger that only God rules. “You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them” (Psalm 89:9). The Psalms tell of merchants who “went out to sea in ships, conducting trade on the mighty waters” and there “saw the works of the LORD, and His wonders in the deep” (Psalm 107:23-24).

And the kindness of a foreign officer to God's servant recalls the warden who showed favour to Joseph in prison (Genesis 39:21).
passages.asks: Paul set out for Rome as a prisoner, but with a friend beside him and a kind officer over him. Ask who has been given to you for the hard stretches of your life, and whether you have thanked God for them. And ask whether you can be like Julius: someone with a little power who uses it to be kind.

passages.happening:
Much time has passed, and sailing has become dangerous, “because it was after the Fast” (verse 9). Paul warns them: “Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well” (verse 10). But the centurion listens to the pilot and the ship's owner instead (verse 11).

Fair Havens is not a good harbour to spend the winter in, so most decide to sail on and try to reach Phoenix, a harbour of Crete facing both southwest and northwest, and winter there (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
‘The Fast’ is the Day of Atonement, the one fast day the Law of Moses commanded, which falls in the autumn. To Luke's readers it was a date as clear as a season.

Ships kept to a season. Vegetius, a Roman writer of the late fourth century, long after Paul, gives the rule sailors had inherited: the safest sailing ran from late May to mid-September, the risky months lay on either side, and from about 11 November to 10 March the sea was treated as closed. Some historians have shown that ships did sail in winter when profit or need pushed them, so the rule was a habit, not a law. But everyone on board knew they were late.

Paul's warning was the kind of judgment an experienced traveller would make, not a vision. He had sailed often, and he had been shipwrecked three times already (2 Corinthians 11:25). The centurion trusted the pilot and the owner instead, which is what most people would have done. They were the experts, and the owner had a cargo to deliver.

Phoenix was a better harbour further west along the coast of Crete. Where exactly it was is debated. Two places on either side of one cape have been proposed, and readers take Luke's description of which way it faced in more than one way.
passages.ot:
The Fast is the Day of Atonement of the Law: “On the tenth day of the seventh month, you shall humble yourselves” (Leviticus 16:29). It was the day the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement for the people.

And the Proverbs know the danger of ignoring wise counsel: “The prudent see danger and take cover, but the simple keep going and suffer the consequences” (Proverbs 22:3).
passages.asks: Paul's advice was sound, and the experts outvoted him. Ask how you weigh advice when the experts and a wise friend disagree. And ask whether you have ever pressed on with a plan you were warned against because you were in a hurry, or because money was waiting at the other end.

passages.t: The Northeaster, and the loss of hope
passages.happening:
A gentle south wind begins to blow, and they think they have their chance. They weigh anchor and sail along close to the coast of Crete (verse 13). But soon a violent wind called the Northeaster sweeps down from the island (verse 14). The ship is caught and cannot head into the wind, so they give way and are driven along (verse 15).

In the shelter of a small island called Cauda they barely manage to secure the lifeboat (verse 16). They haul it up and use ropes to brace the ship. Fearing they will run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lower the sea anchor and are driven along (verse 17). The next day they begin to throw the cargo overboard (verse 18), and on the third day they throw out the ship's tackle with their own hands (verse 19). For many days neither sun nor stars appear, and the storm rages on. “We abandoned all hope of being saved” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
A gentle south wind looked like exactly what they needed to run west along the coast to Phoenix. Then the weather turned.

The Greek name of the storm is Euraquilo, which the Berean Standard Bible translates ‘the Northeaster’. The word seems to join a Greek word for the east wind with a Latin word for the north wind. It came down off the mountains of Crete and drove the ship out to sea.

Luke's sailing detail is unusually exact. The crew hauled in the small boat that was usually towed behind. They passed ropes or cables around the hull to hold the timbers together, as sailors once did in a bad storm. They lowered something to slow their drift: the Greek word is general, and it may mean a sea anchor or some of the ship's gear. They feared the Syrtis, shallow sandbanks off the coast of Libya, far to the south, which sailors dreaded. Then they threw out the cargo and the tackle to lighten the ship.

In the nineteenth century a Scottish scholar and yachtsman, James Smith, studied the voyage closely in The Voyage and Shipwreck of St. Paul (1848). He reckoned that a ship drifting in such a gale would take about two weeks to cover the distance from Cauda to Malta, which fits Luke's ‘fourteenth night’ (verse 27). Many historians of ancient sailing have found Luke's account believable, though not every detail is agreed.

No sun and no stars meant no way to tell where they were. Ancient sailors steered by the sky. ‘We abandoned all hope of being saved.’ The writer includes himself. Even the believers on board had given up.
passages.ot:
The storm recalls Jonah's: “the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart” (Jonah 1:4). Then too the sailors “threw the ship's cargo into the sea to lighten the load” (Jonah 1:5). But Jonah was running from God, and the storm came because of him. Paul is going where God sent him, and the storm comes anyway.

The Psalms describe exactly this: sailors whose “courage melted in their anguish” and who “reeled and staggered like drunkards, and all their skill was useless” (Psalm 107:26-27).
passages.asks: ‘We abandoned all hope.’ The believers on the ship felt it too. Ask whether you have ever been in a storm so long that you gave up hope, and what you would have wanted someone to say to you then. And notice that this storm hit a man who was doing exactly what God told him. Ask whether you expect obedience to keep you out of storms.

passages.t: ‘Take courage’: Paul's word from the angel
passages.happening:
The men have gone a long time without food. Paul stands up among them. He reminds them that they should have taken his advice and not sailed from Crete (verse 21). “But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship” (verse 22).

Last night, he says, an angel of the God he belongs to and serves stood beside him (verse 23) and said, “Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And look, God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you” (verse 24). “So take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen just as He told me” (verse 25). But they must run aground on some island (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Paul's first words sound like ‘I told you so’, but they have a purpose. He had been right before, so they have reason to listen to him now.

Then he speaks of the God ‘whose I am and whom I serve’, to a ship full of sailors and soldiers who worshipped many gods. He does not hide whose servant he is.

The angel's message has two parts. First, a promise for Paul: ‘you must stand before Caesar’. It is the same ‘must’ the Lord spoke in the barracks in Jerusalem (23:11). God's plan for Paul has not been washed away by the storm. Second, a gift: ‘God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Many readers think this means Paul had been praying for them. Two hundred and seventy-six people will live because God is keeping a promise to one prisoner.

The promise does not cancel the danger. They will still lose the ship. They will still run aground. The promise is that they will come through it, not that they will avoid it.

And Paul's courage rests on one thing: ‘I believe God that it will happen just as He told me.’ That is faith in its simplest form: trusting that God will do what he said.
passages.ot:
‘Do not be afraid’ is the word God speaks again and again to those he sends. To Isaiah's hearers he said, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you” (Isaiah 43:2). The Psalms sing, “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble” (Psalm 46:1).

And God sparing many for the sake of one has an Old Testament pattern: “the LORD blessed the Egyptian's household on account of him” (Genesis 39:5), because of Joseph.
passages.asks: Paul said, ‘I believe God that it will happen just as He told me.’ Ask what God has promised in Scripture that you find hardest to believe in the middle of a storm. And notice that the people on that ship were spared because one prisoner prayed for them. Ask who you are praying for, and whether you believe it matters.

passages.t: Near land, and the sailors' escape stopped
passages.happening:
On the fourteenth night they are still being driven across the Adriatic Sea. About midnight the sailors sense land is near (verse 27). They take soundings: twenty fathoms, then fifteen (verse 28). Afraid of hitting rocks, they drop four anchors from the stern and pray for daylight (verse 29).

Then the sailors try to escape. Pretending to put out anchors from the bow, they lower the lifeboat into the sea (verse 30). Paul tells the centurion and soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved” (verse 31). So the soldiers cut the ropes of the lifeboat and let it drift away (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
‘The Adriatic Sea’ in ancient use meant more than the narrow sea between Italy and the Balkans. It covered the wider sea between Greece, Italy and Sicily, where they were drifting.

A fathom is about six feet, or nearly two metres. Twenty fathoms, then fifteen: the sea floor was rising fast. Anchoring from the stern kept the ship's front pointed toward the shore, ready to run onto it at daylight. And they ‘prayed for daybreak’. Everyone on board was praying now.

Then the sailors try to save themselves in the only boat and leave everyone else behind. Paul sees it and warns the centurion. Without the sailors, no one would be able to handle the ship in the morning.

Here is the puzzle. God had promised that everyone would live (verse 24). Why, then, did it matter whether the sailors stayed? Christians answer in different ways. Those who stress God's sovereign rule, such as Reformed Christians, say that God ordains the means as well as the end: the promise was certain, and it would be kept through the sailors staying and working the ship. Those who stress human freedom, such as Arminian and Wesleyan Christians, say that God's promises often come with conditions that real human choices can affect. These notes do not choose between them.

Both readings agree on what Paul did. He did not treat God's promise as a reason to do nothing. He watched, warned, and acted. The promise was kept through faithful action, not apart from it.
passages.ot:
Scripture often joins God's sure promise with human effort. When Nehemiah's enemies threatened Jerusalem, “we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night” (Nehemiah 4:9). Prayer and the guard went together.

And the Psalms tell of sailors in the storm who “cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He brought them out of their distress” and “guided them to the harbor they desired” (Psalm 107:28-30).
passages.asks: God promised that all would live, and Paul still kept watch and spoke up. Ask whether you ever use God's promises as a reason to do nothing. And the sailors tried to save themselves and leave the rest. Ask whether, when things go badly, you think first of your own way out or of the people beside you.

passages.t: Paul breaks bread in the storm
passages.happening:
Just before dawn Paul urges them all to eat. “Today is your fourteenth day in constant suspense, without taking any food” (verse 33). He urges them to eat for their own good, “because not a single hair of your head will be lost” (verse 34).

Then he takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it and begins to eat (verse 35). They are all encouraged and eat too (verse 36). There are 276 people on board (verse 37). When they have eaten their fill, they lighten the ship by throwing the grain into the sea (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Fourteen days without proper food: too seasick, too frightened, too busy to eat. Paul, the prisoner, takes charge, and he does it with a meal.

He takes bread, gives thanks to God ‘in front of them all’, breaks it and eats. The words are the words of an ordinary Jewish meal, where the one at the head gives thanks and breaks the bread. They are also close to the words of Jesus feeding the crowds and at the Last Supper. Readers take this in different ways. Most think it was an ordinary meal, eaten with a believer's thanksgiving, by people of many faiths and none. Some hear a deliberate echo of the Lord's Supper. Luke does not say which.

What is plain is the effect. A man who believes God gives thanks before everyone, and 276 frightened people take heart and eat.

The number, 276, is large but possible for a big grain ship. A few copies give a smaller number, about seventy-six; most read 276.

Then they throw the grain overboard, the very cargo the voyage was for. The owner who had wanted to press on from Crete now watches his profit go into the sea.
passages.ot:
God feeding his people when they are worn out is an old story. When Elijah lay down in despair, an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat” (1 Kings 19:5), and he found bread baked over hot coals.

‘Not a single hair’ echoes a promise made long before. When King Saul was ready to put his son Jonathan to death, the people said, “not a hair of his head will fall to the ground” (1 Samuel 14:45).
passages.asks: In the middle of a storm, Paul gave thanks for bread in front of everyone. Ask whether you give thanks to God openly, in ordinary moments, where others can see. And notice that his faith showed itself in a very practical act: telling hungry people to eat. Ask what the practical form of faith looks like in your own hard place.

passages.t: The wreck, and everyone brought safely to land
passages.happening:
At daylight they do not recognise the land, but they see a bay with a sandy beach, and decide to run the ship onto it if they can (verse 39). They cut away the anchors, loosen the ropes that hold the rudders, hoist the foresail to the wind, and make for the beach (verse 40). But the ship strikes a sandbar. The front sticks fast and will not move, and the back is broken up by the pounding waves (verse 41).

The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, so that none can swim away and escape (verse 42). But the centurion, wanting to save Paul's life, stops them. He orders those who can swim to jump overboard first and get to land (verse 43), and the rest to follow on planks and pieces of the ship. “In this way everyone was brought safely to land” (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Ancient ships were steered by two large oars at the back, which Luke calls ‘rudders’. Now the ropes that held them are loosened so the crew can steer. The foresail is raised to drive the ship toward the beach. Then the ship hits a bank of sand or mud before the beach, sticks fast, and begins to break apart.

The soldiers' plan sounds brutal, and it was. But it came from fear. A Roman guard could be punished, even with death, if his prisoners escaped. Acts has shown this twice: Herod had Peter's guards executed (12:19), and the jailer at Philippi was about to kill himself when he thought his prisoners had fled (16:27). The soldiers would rather kill the prisoners than answer for them.

The centurion, Julius, stops them. Luke gives his reason: ‘wanting to spare Paul's life’. The kindness he showed Paul at Sidon (verse 3), and the respect Paul earned on the voyage, now save not only Paul but every prisoner on board.

And so the promise is kept, though not in a tidy way. The ship is lost. People swim, or cling to planks and broken pieces of wood. But ‘everyone was brought safely to land’. Luke's Greek word for ‘brought safely’ comes from the same root as ‘saved’ in verses 20 and 31. All 276, sailors, soldiers and prisoners, owe their lives to the God of one prisoner who believed him.
passages.ot: Coming through the waters alive is one of Scripture's great pictures of rescue. Israel passed through the sea on dry ground (Exodus 14:29). Jonah, thrown into the sea, prayed, “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me” (Jonah 2:2). And God promises through Isaiah, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you” (Isaiah 43:2).
passages.asks: Everyone reached land, some swimming, some on broken planks. Ask whether you can trust God's promise to bring you through even when it does not look the way you imagined. And a centurion's respect for one man saved many lives. Ask how your faithfulness might protect people who will never know it.
